P004.text: Recent years have witnessed increased use of large language models (LLMs) in clinical language tasks, including patient education, clinical documentation, and administrative work. Many of these applications rely on identifying relevant information from electronic health record (EHR) data before it can be summarized, analyzed, or used in another task. Reliable extraction from those notes is therefore an important step in applying LLMs to oncology care and research.

P006.text: Although EHRs contain structured fields, it is estimated that 80% of clinical data exist in unstructured form (Kong, 2019), and a large proportion of clinically relevant information is encoded in free-text narratives (Wiest et al., 2024). Oncology notes are particularly challenging because a patient can have a complex medical history that contains multiple diagnoses, prior and future treatments, and changes in disease status. Key information may be distributed across different sections, expressed with uncertainty, linked through complex timelines, or even documented incorrectly. As commonly seen in real-world practice, copied-forward laboratory, imaging, and genomic results lengthen notes and further complicate the extraction task. A decade-long study of outpatient documentation found that notes became longer and more redundant, with much of the increase attributable to templates or copied and pasted text (Rule et al., 2021). LLMs must therefore not only identify the relevant information, but also determine its relationship to the patient's current diseases.

P008.text: Currently, LLMs can assist with this task, but the output does not ensure that the extracted information is fully faithful to the original note. Models may generate false information, omit details, confuse historical findings, or infer plausible content where the note does not provide it. These errors can be difficult for human reviewers to detect. Commercial LLMs have been evaluated for clinical note extraction, but performance remains variable. The use of commercial models also raises privacy and governance concerns. The potential transmission of patients' protected health information (PHI) to externally hosted services can introduce institutional and patient concerns related to data processing, retention, and HIPAA compliance. A locally deployed open-weight model can process notes without sending PHI to outside sources. However, local models alone do not resolve extraction errors.

P010.text: Local open-weight models are smaller, and their performance varies with model size. Recent studies suggest that the performance of LLMs depends not only on the model but also on how the model is used. Several strategies have been used to improve clinical extraction. Fine-tuning adapts the model to a medical task by continuing to train the model on domain-specific knowledge. This process is usually time-consuming and requires large datasets. Alternatively, prompt design, task decomposition, and verification can improve extraction accuracy without retraining the model. Expert review can guide the process by identifying recurring errors and refining the extraction workflow (Huang et al., 2024; Hein et al., 2025). Less is known about how to turn expert feedback into a workflow for note extraction.

P012.text: We use the term inference harness to describe the execution workflow surrounding an LLM, including the sequence of extraction tasks, checks, and clinical rules applied without changing the model weights. We developed a locally deployable framework for extracting information from real-world unstructured oncology notes. The framework combines structured inference-harness engineering with a physician-preference-guided development loop. Our results showed that the harness output was favored over a single-prompt baseline and that we could adapt the harness to a second cancer type through model-assisted development.

P017.text: The study comprised two development stages followed by an independent clinical evaluation. During breast-cancer development, a physician coauthor and the model-development investigators iteratively reviewed extraction outputs, identified recurring errors, and revised the inference harness. The framework was then adapted to pancreatic cancer using model-assisted review, without clinician review of pancreatic-cancer outputs. The model-assisted review used the error categories and clinical distinctions established during breast-cancer development to identify potential errors and propose revisions, which the investigators assessed and regression-tested.

P019.text: The final harness was compared with a single-prompt baseline using the same frozen model and field schema on 40 expert-annotated CORAL notes. Four physicians completed system-label-masked A/B evaluations across both cancer types. A secondary technical ablation compared four stages of inference-harness development using blinded LLM review.

workflow-cross-reference.text: The study workflow is shown in Figure 1.

P022.text: We used the CORAL dataset, a PhysioNet dataset of 40 deidentified medical oncology notes obtained from the University of California, San Francisco. The development pool contains 100 breast-cancer and 100 pancreatic-cancer notes without expert annotation. The untouched holdout test set contains 20 expert-annotated notes for each cancer type. Access requires the PhysioNet credentialing and data-use process described by the dataset authors.

revision-annotation-use.text: The expert annotations for the holdout notes were not provided to either system, were not used to develop the inference harness, and were not used to calculate the primary physician-preference endpoint.

P025.text: We used Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct-AWQ served locally through vLLM. The baseline model made one model call per note and returned the complete target schema. In the clinician review, the baseline model and the harness model used the same field definitions and output contract.

P028.text: The harness extracted clinical information in multiple steps because different fields required different clinical context and reasoning. First, field-specific prompts independently identified the visit context, cancer diagnosis, laboratory results, objective findings, active medications, and recent treatment changes. Information extracted in earlier steps was then used to guide subsequent assessments. For example, cancer stage and metastatic status provide context for treatment intent, while current therapy and clinical findings provide context for treatment response. Plan fields were extracted primarily from the Assessment and Plan section. The harness first used deterministic patterns to identify this section. If the section could not be identified, the model made up to three attempts to locate and reproduce the relevant text, with each attempt checked against the original note. If all attempts failed, the system omitted plan-specific extraction rather than generate information not present in the source note.

P030.text: Each model output passes through five verification stages. The first two address structural errors through JSON formatting repair and schema validation. The remaining three assess clinical content: semantic alignment, a faithfulness check, and temporal filtering. These verification stages ensure that the extracted information is complete, clinically relevant, and consistent with the source note. See Table 1.

P032.text: JSON formatting repair when parsing fails.

P033.text: Schema validation to detect incorrect or leaked keys.

P034.text: Specificity and semantic alignment checks to identify vague or off-task answers.

P035.text: Faithfulness trimming to remove clearly unsupported or contradictory content while retaining supported information.

P036.text: Temporal filtering to remove completed or historical events from future-plan fields.

P038.text: We included clinical rules to address recurring extraction errors. For example, these rules helped the system distinguish regional lymph node involvement from distant metastases, suspected metastatic disease from confirmed metastatic disease, and active anticancer treatment from supportive or home medications. They also prevented disease changes documented before treatment initiation from being misclassified as a treatment response. The system returned supporting excerpts from the original clinical note when available.

figure-1::caption.text: Figure 1. Development, transfer, and evaluation pathway. Breast-cancer physician review informed the inference harness. The failure history and clinical rubric then supported author-controlled PDAC adaptation without target-domain physician review of outputs. Four physicians compared the final harness with the same-model single-prompt baseline on the 40-note holdout set.

T1R2C2.text: Extracting multiple fields in a single prompt may lead to missing or mixed information

T1R2C3.text: Separate current medication from previous and future treatment plans.

T1R3C3.text: Use metastatic status when interpreting stage and response

T1R4C2.text: The model returns medically related answers that do not address the target question

T1R4C3.text: Remove a future treatment plan from current response

T1R5C2.text: The model infers a conclusion that is not supported by the note

T1R5C3.text: Keep a lesion classified as suspected rather than label it as confirmed when a biopsy is pending

T1R6C2.text: Confusion among past, current, and future information.

T1R6C3.text: Remove a completed scan from the imaging plan

T1R7C2.text: A medication may be misclassified when its clinical role is unclear from the drug name alone

T1R7C3.text: Separate anticancer drugs from home and supportive medications

T1R8C2.text: Stage, nodes, and distant disease become inconsistent

T1R8C3.text: Keep axillary nodes regional rather than distant

T1R9C2.text: A reviewer cannot trace an extracted value

T1R9C3.text: Return the supporting sentence from the note

P057.text: Breast-cancer development used all 100 development notes. Early and targeted iterations used smaller subsets to shorten the feedback cycle, while major and final runs covered all 100 notes to detect less frequent errors and check for regression. A physician reviewed selected outputs, and the investigator compared flagged outputs with the complete source note, grouped recurring errors, and translated them into general changes to prompts, verification logic, or deterministic rules. This physician author did not participate in the final evaluation. These changes were retained only after testing on affected examples. The objective was to encode recurring clinical distinctions rather than case-specific corrections. For example, an error in which axillary nodal disease was classified as distant metastasis motivated a general regional-node rule. An error in which a planned drug was listed as active therapy motivated a temporal medication rule. This process did not produce a conventional supervised training set, and the model weights were not updated.

P060.text: The harness developed from breast-cancer notes was further adapted to pancreatic cancer using 100 additional pancreatic-cancer notes. No clinician reviewed pancreatic-cancer outputs during this stage. Instead, an external LLM (ChatGPT) was used to organize the clinical error categories that were found during breast-cancer development into a structured review rubric. The Qwen pipeline generated structured outputs, and a rubric-guided Qwen reviewer compared these outputs with the full pancreatic notes to identify potential errors and areas for improvement. Investigators reviewed the errors, implemented selected revisions to prompts, clinical rules, or workflow logic, and kept those changes only after regression testing.

P061.text: The adaptation retained the core framework while introducing pancreatic-cancer-specific modifications, particularly for disease terminology, treatment regimens, and post-processing rules. The framework thus preserved its core approach to error detection and correction while accommodating differences between the two cancer types.

P062.text: Clinical evaluation data collection and scoring rubric

P063.text: The clinical evaluation presented the source note and two structured outputs through a system-label-masked A/B interface. Evaluators selected A better, B better, or tie for each field. They were blinded to the identities of the systems. The physician who participated in the human-in-the-loop development was not one of the final evaluators. Before evaluating the test set, the authors designated seven core fields as clinically important for understanding disease status and current management. See Supplementary Table S1.

revision-evaluation-package.text: Output A was always the inference-harness output, and output B was always the single-prompt baseline output. Physicians were blinded to these system identities. Source attribution was available only in the inference-harness output, so the comparison evaluated the full system output packages rather than any isolated component.

P067.text: We ran a secondary technical ablation on the same 20 breast-cancer and 20 pancreatic-cancer benchmark notes. All four conditions used Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct-AWQ, greedy decoding, and the same 31-field output contract. Attribution, tool calling, and letter generation were disabled.

T2R1C2.text: A single-prompt baseline with one model call per note.

T2R2C2.text: Decomposed field extraction with cross-field routing, bounded Assessment and Plan retry, and the shared format and schema safeguards.

T2R3C2.text: Condition B plus the semantic, faithfulness, and temporal verification gates.

T2R4C2.text: Condition C plus deterministic inline processing and the complete POST-hook layer used by the full inference harness.

P073.text: We compared adjacent configurations (A vs B, B vs C, and C vs D), yielding 120 paired comparisons across 40 notes. An AI judge (Codex) was given only the source note and the two outputs. The judge had no access to the project code, development history, prior evaluations, or system identities. The judge was instructed to prioritize source faithfulness, then completeness, and to use TIE when differences were minor or offsetting. We compared adjacent configurations using two-sided exact sign tests, excluding ties.

P076.text: For the physician evaluation, interrater agreement was assessed pairwise using exact agreement and Cohen's κ for each evaluator pair. Results from the 8 completed clinician-by-cancer evaluations were summarized separately. Pooled counts were reported descriptively and were not treated as independent field-level observations.

P078.text: For the primary inferential analysis, tied comparisons were excluded, and each remaining directional judgment was coded according to whether it favored the harness or the baseline. We fit a population-averaged logistic generalized estimating equation (GEE) with an exchangeable working correlation structure at the note level to account for clustering of repeated field-level judgments within the same note. Evaluator was included as a fixed effect, and cancer type was additionally included in the overall model. Cancer-specific models adjusted for evaluator.

P080.text: The primary outcome was the adjusted probability of harness preference among directional judgments. Predicted probabilities were standardized over the observed covariate distribution, and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using the delta method on the logit scale. Adjusted probabilities and adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were reported.

P082.text: For sensitivity analyses, we refitted the overall model four times after excluding one physician at a time. We also retained tied judgments by coding harness, tie, and baseline preferences as 1, 0, and −1, respectively, and calculated the mean net preference margin with 95% CIs using note-clustered sandwich standard errors. Finally, we aggregated field-level preferences within each note and performed an exact two-sided sign test comparing positive and negative note-level margins.

core-field-statistical-analysis.text: Exploratory core-field analysis used one joint population-averaged logistic GEE on 495 directional core judgments. Field, physician, and cancer type were fixed effects; repeated judgments were clustered by note with an exchangeable working correlation. Field-specific probabilities were standardized over the physician and cancer distribution observed for that field. Breast type and receptor status applied only to breast-cancer notes. Ties were excluded. These estimates describe preference rather than accuracy, and no pairwise field tests or multiplicity claims were made.

P085.text: All 4 physicians evaluated both cancer types and completed 2,160 comparisons. Across 2,160 required note-field judgments, the harness was preferred 699 times, 1,290 comparisons were ties, and the baseline was preferred 171 times. See Table 3, Table 4, and Figure 2. These correspond to 32.36%, 59.72%, and 7.92% of all judgments. Among the 870 directional judgments, the crude harness share was 80.34% (note-cluster-robust 95% CI 76.14% to 83.96%).

P086.text: For breast-cancer notes, all four physicians independently favored the harness. Their pooled breast result was 363 harness preferences, 80 baseline preferences, and 677 ties. The first physician's per-note result was 18 harness wins, one baseline win, and one tie. The second and third physicians each recorded a harness win in all 20 notes. The fourth recorded 16 harness wins, two baseline wins, and two ties. When the four breast evaluations were combined within each note, all 20 notes had a positive harness-minus-baseline margin (Supplementary Figure S1).

P087.text: For pancreatic cancer notes, the evaluations produced 336 harness preferences, 91 baseline preferences, and 613 ties. The harness had a positive pooled margin in 19 pancreatic notes and a negative margin in one.

figure-2::caption.text: Figure 2. Physician preferences across eight physician-by-cancer evaluations. Panel A retains harness, baseline, and tie judgments. Panel B shows the harness share among directional judgments.

P092.text: The adjusted probability of a harness preference among directional judgments was 79.98% (95% CI 75.75% to 83.63%). The breast-cancer estimate was 81.66% (95% CI, 76.02% to 86.21%), and the pancreatic-cancer estimate was 78.15% (95% CI, 71.47% to 83.62%). The same standardized estimates on the odds scale were 3.995 overall (95% CI, 3.12 to 5.11; p < 0.05), 4.45 for breast cancer (95% CI, 3.17 to 6.25; p < 0.05), and 3.576 for pancreatic cancer (95% CI, 2.51 to 5.11; p < 0.05). See Table 5.

table-5::caption.text: Table 5. Adjusted probability of inference-harness preference among directional judgments

P095.text: Sensitivity analyses supported the primary findings. When ties were included, the net preference margin favored the harness (+24.4 percentage points; 95% CI, +20.4 to +28.5). At the note level, the harness was preferred in 39 of 40 cases (97.5%). Results remained consistent when each physician was excluded individually; adjusted harness-preference probabilities ranged from 77.08% to 83.53% (Supplementary Table S3).

agreement-results.text: Pairwise exact agreement ranged from 73.1% to 82.9%, with Cohen's kappa ranging from 0.511 to 0.646 (Figure 3 and Supplementary Table S2).

figure-3::caption.text: Figure 3. Pairwise exact agreement and Cohen's kappa among four physicians in breast cancer and PDAC. Each breast-cancer pair shared 280 judgments, and each PDAC pair shared 260 judgments.

P097.text: Next, we analyzed which questions had the greatest influence on the results. Across the 1,040 evaluations, physicians preferred the harness in 418 comparisons (40.2%), the baseline in 77 (7.4%), and 545 (52.4%) were ties. When ties were excluded, 84.4% favored the harness. The harness was preferred more often than the baseline across all seven fields, with the largest difference seen in identifying active anticancer medications (132 vs 3). Differences were smaller for distant metastasis and breast-cancer type and receptor status, where ties were more common (Figure 4).

figure-4::caption.text: Figure 4. Core-field preference results. Panel A retains the tie-inclusive raw distribution for seven physician-prioritized fields. Panel B shows core-field adjusted harness-preference probabilities with 95% confidence intervals from one joint exploratory GEE fitted to 495 directional core judgments. The model included field, physician, and cancer fixed effects, clustered repeated judgments by note with an exchangeable working correlation, and standardized each field over its observed physician and cancer distribution. Breast type and receptor status applied only to breast-cancer notes. Ties were excluded from Panel B. The estimates report preference, not accuracy. No pairwise field tests or multiplicity claims were made.

P100.text: We also analyzed physician preferences for each individual note to determine whether the overall advantage was consistent across cases. After combining physician ratings for each note, the harness was preferred in all 20 breast-cancer notes and 19 of 20 pancreatic-cancer notes. The overall ratings also favored the harness in each evaluator-by-cancer group. These findings were consistent with the primary analysis and suggest that the observed advantage was not driven by a small number of clinical notes (Supplementary Figure S1).

P109.text: In this study, the inference harness was preferred over a single-prompt baseline using the same underlying LLM. This advantage was observed in both breast and pancreatic cancer and remained consistent across the sensitivity analyses. These findings suggest that a structured inference harness can improve the clinical quality of extracted information without additional model training.

P111.text: Structured extraction can convert long, complex, free-text notes into a compact set of fields that can be checked, searched, and reused downstream. In oncology, this is useful because clinical notes can be complex and contain multiple diagnoses, prior and future treatments, and changes in disease status. Prior studies have demonstrated the potential of LLMs for extracting structured information from clinical notes. However, the CORAL study showed that advanced commercial models could omit information or generate unsupported findings (Sushil et al., 2024). Huang et al. (2024) demonstrated that iterative prompt engineering using ChatGPT via an API could improve extraction of free-text pathology notes. Similarly, Hein et al. (2025) showed that iterative refinement guided by clinicians and systematic error analysis could improve structured extraction and be adapted to other cancer types.

P113.text: Our study built on these studies by using physician feedback to identify recurring errors and develop clinical rules during breast-cancer note development. Rather than producing a large, supervised training set, we used the feedback to develop field-specific prompts, verification steps, and clinical rules. This approach incorporated clinician knowledge into the inference harness and was reused in subsequent extraction tasks. Instead of asking physicians to perform iterative evaluation, we used ChatGPT to organize the established criteria from breast-cancer development, and used Qwen2.5-32B as a judge. LLM-as-a-judge approaches have been reported in prior studies, which showed that LLM judges had high concordance on text-comparison rubrics such as faithfulness and completeness (Gershon et al., 2026). The final harness was preferred over the baseline by independent physician evaluators for pancreatic cancer. This finding suggests that criteria established through physician feedback may be transferable to other cancer types and may reduce the need for repeated physician review during development.

P115.text: One recurring challenge we identified was the interpretation of temporal relationships in oncology notes. Prior studies have reported broader temporal reasoning challenges in clinical notes (Kruse et al., 2025; Kougia et al., 2024). Although the LLM could identify treatment responses documented in the clinical history, it sometimes failed to associate them with the correct disease status. For example, a response to a previous treatment could be incorrectly attributed to the current regimen. This was particularly important for patients who had received multiple lines of therapy, where each treatment response must be associated with the corresponding treatment history. We addressed this issue by incorporating treatment history and temporal context into the extraction process and adding verification steps to align treatment responses with the appropriate regimen. The physician evaluators preferred the harness over the baseline, suggesting that temporal checks could help reduce these errors. 13

P117.text: Our ablation analysis suggested that verification was an important component of the inference harness (Supplementary Figure S2). Adding decomposed extraction alone did not produce an overall improvement, whereas adding layers of verification gates resulted in significantly more favorable evaluations. Additionally, we found that the clinical rules developed from breast cancer did not provide further improvement for pancreatic cancer. This suggests that restrictive rules that performed well in one cancer type may not improve performance in another. More restrictive rules may introduce trade-offs, especially when the terminology or treatment differs between cancer types. For example, some rules developed for breast cancer were specific to estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2 status, which are used to classify breast cancer subtypes but are not applicable to PDAC.14

P119.text: This study has several limitations. First, our primary outcome was physician preference rather than absolute extraction accuracy. A tie could indicate that both systems produced acceptable outputs or that both contained errors. Although physician ratings consistently favored the harness, the evaluation included only four physicians and 40 clinical notes from two cancer types within a single-source dataset. However, these were real clinical notes rather than synthetic cases or model-generated narratives. They contain repeated, copied-forward information, uncertain findings, treatment plans, or even typographical errors that make the extraction task challenging. Nevertheless, further studies are needed to investigate whether the results can be generalized to other cancer types or language models. Second, the exploratory ablation was evaluated by a single non-physician LLM judge and compared cumulative stages rather than individual components (Williams et al., 2026). Therefore, it could not determine the independent contribution of each verification step or clinical rule. Future studies should evaluate extraction accuracy against expert reference standards, include larger and more diverse clinical datasets, and assess whether the harness improves efficiency and reliability in clinical workflows.

revision-model-family-limitation.text: Both systems used the same base-model family, so this study did not evaluate whether the findings generalize across model families.
